title: Chapter 110 – Inner Trial
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Seven months later.

The new clause is eleven lines long, and it was written in the wrong ink.

Jian sees it on the third morning of the ninth month, standing in the colonnade outside the Hall of Weights with a crowd of Silver Leaf disciples pressing round the notice-board. Most of them are reading the rankings. A few, the better prepared, are reading the Rule. Someone has pinned a fresh copy of Article forty-four beside the sheet of names, and a white paper tag with a red stamp: AMENDED, SPRING.

He reads it once. Then he lets his gaze go slack, and opens the Door in Autumn.

It costs two points of CE. He has thirty. The colonnade blurs at the edges, and the paper in front of him sharpens until the characters stand off the page like carved stone. He sees the grain of the fibers. He sees the ink, black and dry, laid down by a clerk's brush in a hand he knows by heart. And under the ink, so faint that he would miss it if he did not know what he was looking for, a thread of cold silver-gray, laid on the paper like a hair.

A Registry hand, he thinks. Spring. Three months after the charter.

The Gate Bearer shall retain the right of the stair only while his standing in the Silver Leaf ranking is among the first ten. A Gate Bearer ranked below the tenth place shall surrender the right of the stair for the following season, pending the next ranking.

He reads it a second time, slowly, with the cold spreading through his chest.

It is a small clause. It is very reasonable. It would pass any floor in the Sect without comment, and no one would think to ask how it came to be written. He has been a Gate Bearer for six years. His standing has been confirmed. The right of the stair, the right to go down into the Dock, to lie on the bench, to read the register, is the thing he has built every plan upon.

And someone has tied it to a ranking.

"You've gone pale," says a dry voice at his shoulder.

Tan Ruyan is standing beside him, in the silver-edged gray, with the jade pin of a Foundation Early in her hair. She is twenty-two now, and taller than she was, and her black braid hangs to her waist. She is reading the notice with the cool absorbed look she gives to ledgers. She does not look at him.

"It's new," she says.

"It is."

"They put it up on the last day of the old season. I saw the clerk." She taps the paper with one fingertip. "Nobody else did. The Examiner was out of the Hall."

"Which Examiner?"

"The new one." Her voice is quite flat. "Cheng Yun was moved to the Court bench after the charter. The Hall of Weights has had five different men since, in seven months. Each of them was a very pleasant person with a very small ledger." She turns her head, finally, and her dark eyes meet his. "You are eleventh on the list."

He looks. His name is there, on the board, in neat black characters. Eleventh.

"I was fifth at the midsummer."

"You were. Then the Hall re-measured the cohort." She says it carefully. "Your Qi reading was entered as Foundation Early. Your soul as step four."

"That is wrong."

"I know it is wrong. You are a Foundation Middle. Everyone saw the sky." Her mouth is a hard line. "I have been to the Hall three times to ask about it. They say it is a matter of the Mirror. They say the Mirror is old."

"And the tenth place?"

"Is mine."

She says it without any emphasis. The words fall between them like a dropped coin, and for a moment neither moves.

* * *

The Inner Trial lasts four days, and it is a thing of paper, and sweat, and small cruelties.

It is held every season, on the lawns and in the halls of the Inner Court, and it is the one test every Silver Leaf must pass. Not a duel. Not a tournament. A catalog. Four measurements: of the hands, the mind, the body, and the Qi. Each is scored out of a hundred, by examiners who sit at long tables in the shade, and the four scores are added, and the sums are ranked, and the ranks are posted on a board.

The first day is the Pill Hall.

He walks into it at dawn with a sense of coming home. The great room smells of ash and camphor. A hundred small furnaces stand in rows, each with a number, each with a stool and a stone mortar and a rack of herbs. At the head of the hall, behind a long table, the examiners wait: a row of gray-robed Elders from the Pill Hall, and in the center, with a plum in each fist, round and rumpled and radiating satisfaction, Bai.

"Furnace thirty-seven," says the old man, without looking up. "Do not touch the second. You know why."

"Yes, Elder."

"Begin."

The task is a Rank Two tonic, forty doses, from raw herbs, in one hour. He has done it a hundred times. His hands move without his mind. The pestle falls, the powder floats, the furnace takes the heat. He does not think of the notice-board. He does not think of the ink. He thinks of the weight of the root in his palm, the hush of the herbs in the bowl, the old quiet pleasure of a thing done well.

At the end of the hour he sets forty sealed doses on the table, and Bai picks one up, and sniffs it, and puts it down.

"Ninety-eight," says the old Elder. "I took two off for the wax. It was thick." He chews. "Second place. Ye Linfeng did a ninety-nine, and she is a Rank Three. I'd have given you the hundred, but she would have complained."

"Thank you, Elder."

"Do not thank me. Go and eat. You've got a long way to fall."

* * *

The second day is the stones.

It is the Formation Hall, a dim vaulted chamber under the Sutra Hall, where sixty flat slabs of gray granite are laid on the floor in a grid. Each slab is carved with a different pattern of lines. Each disciple is given a number, and an hour, and a single task: read the pattern, find the flaw, and name the stone that will break the array.

He kneels on the cold floor in front of his slab and studies it.

It is a lovely thing. A square of dark stone, three feet to the side, cut with fine lines that run in nine concentric rings, each broken at a different point. The pattern is old. He knows the tradition: a Nine-Ring Lock, a defensive array of the Coral Gate, taught in the second year of Silver Leaf. There should be a flaw in the third ring. A place where the line is a hair too thin.

He finds it in four minutes.

Then he lets his eyes go soft, and opens the Door in Autumn.

It is a precaution. He tells himself so. It costs two points. He has twenty-eight. But he has had a feeling since the colonnade, a cold wire in his gut that will not go away, and the only way to quiet it is to look.

The slab sharpens. The lines stand up from the granite in bright relief. And across the center, laid like a spider's web over the fifth and sixth rings, so fine that he can see it only from the side, runs a thread of silver-gray.

He sits very still.

It's been seeded, he thinks. The stone is wrong.

He looks closer. The thread runs between two lines that are meant to be separate, joining them at a point where no joint exists. It turns a flawed array into a sound one. If he names the third ring as the flaw, as every textbook would, the Examiner will check his answer against the key, and the key will say the flaw is in the sixth, and he will be marked wrong.

A trap. His breath is slow and steady. They want me to fail by being right.

He looks up. At the far end of the hall, on a high stool, sits a young man in a gray robe with a brush in his hand. He is writing something. His face is bland. His hair is neatly oiled. And at the base of his skull, if Jian turns his head just so, there is a cold bright point, small as a pearl.

He lowers his eyes.

Write the answer, he thinks. The true one. And mark it with the margin.

He takes the brush. He writes: Third ring, fourth segment. Flaw: line thin. NOTE: a foreign filament crosses the fifth and sixth rings at the center. It is not part of the original array. If it is part of the test, I request its provenance be recorded. He signs it with his token and lays it face up on the slab.

It takes the clerk three minutes to read. When he does, his pen stops.

* * *

Feng is waiting in the disciples' court that night, sitting on the well-curb with a lantern between his boots.

He is twenty-nine now, broad through the shoulders, with the stubborn Lin jaw and a Foundation Middle's slow settled breath. He has been a Court runner, a Gate Bearer's escort, and for two years a quiet fixture on the Hall of Weights roster, carrying scrolls for clerks who forget he can read. He stands when Jian comes in, and does not smile.

"The clerk on the stone," he says. "The young one, with the oiled hair. His name is Pei. He has been in the Hall for eight months. I looked him up."

"And?"

"He has no patron on file. No family house. No Sutra Hall entry before the spring." Feng's voice is low and even. "He was transferred from the outer registry, by a form with no seal. The form was filed by a man who does not exist."

"You are sure."

"I carried the form to the archive myself." He turns the lantern down. "I did not know what it was. I only knew the paper. Plum bark. A black square where the seal should be."

Jian sits on the curb beside him. The stones are cold through his leggings. Above the roofs, the stars are hard and white.

"Do not go near him again," he says.

"I am not a child."

"I know. That is why I am saying it." He keeps his eyes on the lantern. "They have placed a man in the Hall because they wanted a rank moved by six points. Not eleven. Not twenty. Six. It is the smallest amount that works. Whoever is doing this is patient, and careful, and does not want anyone hurt. If you are seen near him, it will become a different kind of careful."

Feng is silent for a long moment.

"You could just tell the Arbiter what you saw," he says at last.

"I could."

"But you won't."

"No."

His brother nods, slowly, as if hearing something he has already known. He picks up the lantern. At the gate of the court he stops, and without turning, says, "The clan stands behind whatever you decide. Father said to tell you. He said it twice, so I would not forget."

* * *

On the third day, Kuang hits him for an hour, and he comes in third.

The Iron Bone trial is held on the frozen lawn, in a hard bright morning, with the disciples in lines and the tutors walking behind them with poles. It is simple. A man stands in the stance, and he is struck, and the Examiner counts. He stays standing until he falls, or the pole breaks, or the hour is done. Ten disciples last the hour. Of those, Jian takes the blows on his shoulders and back without a sound, and the pole bounces off with a clean ring.

At the end of it Kuang lowers her weapon and regards him with her flat eyes.

"Third," she says. "You could be first. You hold back."

"I do not wish to be seen."

"You are seen already." She grunts. "Eat more. You're a bag of sticks." She hesitates, a rare thing, and her scarred jaw works once. "The pole that hit you in the ninth round was mine. It did not feel like hitting a man of Foundation Early. I thought you should know I noticed."

He says nothing. There is nothing safe to say. She seems to expect that, and walks away across the frozen grass without another word.

It is the most she has ever said to him in company. He bows. He turns away. And at the edge of the lawn he finds Tan Ruyan standing alone in the thin sunlight, her hands folded behind her back, watching him with an expression he cannot read.

* * *

The fourth day is the Mirror, and the Mirror lies.

It is the Hall of Weights again, the long black room with the bronze disc turning on its plinth. The Silver Leaf line up in the cold morning, barefoot, and step onto the plate in turn. The disc hums. The three rings of light rise in the air: white, red, blue. A clerk reads them out. Another writes. Jian watches from the end of the line, and he counts, and when it is his turn he walks to the plinth in silence, and steps on.

The bronze is cold.

The light rises. White. Red. Blue.

Qi, says the reading clerk, in a high bright voice, Foundation Early. Step five.

He does not speak. He feels the dozens of eyes on his back. He closes his own and opens the Door in Autumn, and in the dark behind his lids the world goes quiet and brilliant. The disc turns beneath him. Its rings are three loops of light, perfect and clear. And across the second ring, the red, a thread of silver-gray has been laid, so cunningly that it looks like part of the metal. It bends the light a hair's breadth, no more, and drops a full step.

He opens his eyes.

Body, the clerk reads. Qi Refining peak. Step four. A pause. Soul, Qi Refining peak. Step four.

It is wrong. All three. The thread has been laid on every ring.

He stands very still. He knows what he is. He knows the sea of Qi in his base, the weight of it, the slow deep turning. He knows that the Mirror has been tampered with by a hand that knows its workings, a hand that has had seven months and five Examiners to prepare. He knows that he could say so, here, now, in front of two hundred people, and be right.

He would also have to say how he knows.

Thread. Silver-gray. Visible only to the Door in Autumn.

He would be asked what the Door in Autumn is. He would be asked who taught it to him. He would be asked, by the Examiner, by the Arbiter, by every person in the Inner Court who has a cousin on the Registry's payroll, what manner of man could see a thread no Mirror had ever shown.

He steps off the plate.

"Thank you," he says, to the clerk. And he walks out of the Hall of Weights into the cold white light, with his name already being copied into the ledger in the wrong hand.

* * *

Between the third day and the fourth, he goes down to the Dock.

He has the right of the stair for one season more, and he takes it. The door at the bottom of the cold passage opens to his palm. The bench waits under its pale lamp, and the register glows on the wall, and he sits in the one chair with his hands flat on his knees.

```
OPERATOR ARK-7 :: SESSION OPEN
CE: 28 / PROVISIONAL
SEAL: 71% (STRAINED)
QUERY: FOREIGN FILAMENT, ASH-GRAY, ON GRANITE?
RESULT: MATCH, 94%. SOURCE CLASS: REGISTRY BLOOD SHADOW, LOW GRADE.
NOTE: FILAMENT IS MOUNTED, NOT WOVEN. IT WAS LAID BY A LIVING HAND.
```

A living hand. He reads the line twice. The thread on the stone was not a trap that a device had sprung. Someone had knelt on that floor with a brush and laid it, line by line, a few nights before the trial. Someone had known which slab he would draw.

He asks the register one more thing.

```
QUERY: CAN THE MIRROR BE CORRECTED FROM HERE?
RESULT: NO. MIRROR IS NOT AN ARK DEVICE.
RESULT: IT MAY BE CORRECTED BY ANY HAND THAT CAN SEE THE FILAMENT.
COST: 2 CE PER RING. SEAL STRAIN: HIGH.
WARNING: ANY CORRECTION WILL BE VISIBLE TO THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR.
```

He sits there for a long time, looking at the last line. He can clean the Mirror. He can walk in tomorrow with the Door open and rub out three threads before the second bell, and every figure will be true. And the hand that laid them will feel it go, as a fisherman feels a line go slack, and will know that someone sees.

He closes the panel.

Not yet, he thinks. Let them think it worked.

He climbs the stair into the dark and does not look back at the door.

* * *

The scores are posted at dusk.

He reads them in the long hall, standing, with a bowl of untouched rice at his elbow. Alchemy, ninety-eight. Formation, seventy-two, marked down for a failure to follow the key. Iron Bone, ninety-one. Qi, sixty. His sum is three hundred and twenty-one. It puts him in eleventh place, by a margin of six points, behind Tan Ruyan, who has scored three hundred and twenty-seven with no flaws at all.

Eleventh.

He can see exactly how it was done. A neat, small, plausible scheme: forty points shaved off the Mirror, a dozen off the stone. A margin of six. Nobody could call it a conspiracy. A matter of an old Mirror and a stubborn pupil. A pattern of honest errors, each one explicable, each one trivial.

And in the next season the stair is closed to me.

He is still standing there, staring at the board, when Ye finds him.

She comes up behind him without a sound, small and gray in her Elder's robe, with her stick tapping. She does not look at the board. She looks at him. She has aged. Her face has the fine, dry, translucent look of old paper held to a lamp. But her pale eyes are sharp.

"You've read the amendment," she says.

"Yes."

"And the Mirror."

"Yes."

"I could appeal," she says. "On your behalf. The Sutra Hall has standing. I could call for an inspection of the Mirror, a re-test, a hearing before the Arbiter. I could make a very great deal of noise."

"And they would find the Mirror sound."

"They would find it sound. It would be sound by the time the Arbiter came." She taps her stick. "The thread would be gone. The stone would be re-cut. The clerk would have been reassigned to the south."

"Unless I can show it."

"Unless you can show it." Her voice drops. "And to show it, you would have to say how you came to see."

He looks at the board. At his name. At Ruyan's, one place above.

"They have made the choice very simple," he says slowly. "Say nothing, and lose the stair for a season. Say everything, and lose the thing that keeps me alive."

"Not alive. Hidden." She corrects him gently. "The Door in Autumn is the one advantage they do not know you have. If you reveal it now, to the floor, in a public hearing, you reveal it to the Keeper. And the Keeper will know exactly how to hide from you."

"A season is a long time."

"Four months." She meets his eyes. "I have counted. The Dock can wait four months. The Door cannot be taken back."

"And if the next season is the same? If the Mirror is wrong again, and the Trial after that?"

"Then you will have four months to find the hand that holds the brush." She lowers her voice further. "Qin Hao has heard of the amendment. He asked me to say that a tied vote is still a vote, and that the Court meets on the first of the month. He did not say what he meant. He seldom does."

He thinks of the narrow face, the folded hands, the sixty years set down on a table. He thinks that of everyone in the Sect, the Gate Elder is the only one who has ever paid for him in advance.

* * *

Tan Ruyan finds him on the Pill Hall steps at the first bell of night.

She has changed from the silver-edged gray into a plain dark robe, and her braid is down. She stands two steps above him with her arms wrapped round herself against the cold, and for the first time since he has known her, she looks her age.

"I have come to give you something," she says.

"What?"

"My place."

He looks up.

"I came tenth. By six points." She says it quietly, her eyes fixed on a point past his shoulder. "I know what you scored, Jian. I know what you should have scored. I have a head for sums." A short, bitter breath. "Three hundred and eighty. You should be first."

"Ruyan—"

"Under Article forty-four, the rank can be ceded. A disciple may yield a place to another, in writing, by leave of the Elder of the Hall. It's an old provision. Seldom used." She takes a folded paper from her sleeve. "I have written it. I have asked Bai to witness. He said he would. He said it was the first sensible thing anyone had done all week."

"You'd lose your own stair rights."

"I have none. I have never gone down." Her mouth twists. "I have a seat on the Court's roll and a family house. I don't need the Dock. You do."

"The Tan house—"

"Will survive." She lifts her chin. "I owe you more than a place, Lin Jian. I owe you a page. A book. Seventeen years of ink. I tore it out and put it in your hand and I have not slept easily since. I would like, just once, to give you something that doesn't cost anyone."

"It costs you."

"It costs me a number." She holds out the paper.

He looks at it. It is a single sheet, folded in thirds, with a red stamp and Bai's cramped signature at the bottom. It is a small thing. It would take two seconds to accept.

It would put her name below the line.

The Registry will see it. They will see that the Tan heir yielded her place to the Gate Bearer, in writing, before a witness. They will see that the House of Tan and the House of Lin are bound by more than a contract. And they will do what they have always done: they will count, and they will mark, and they will wait.

I'd be spending her to buy four months, he thinks.

"Take it," says Ruyan, with a faint, crooked smile. "Before I change my mind."

The night is cold and clear. A star falls behind the ridge. On the Pill Hall steps, in the lamplight, the paper trembles very slightly in her fingers.

He looks at her hand. He looks at his own.

And he thinks of Qin Hao on his stool, and the sixty years in the bowl, and the price of letting someone else pay.
